I'm a freelance illustrator. Here are my March expenses. Sort them into categories and give me a total for the business ones only.

Adobe Creative Cloud subscription - $54.99
Wacom pen nibs - $12.50
Skillshare membership - $13.99
Lunch with a client - $38.20
Netflix - $15.49
USB-C hub - $46.99
Domain renewal for my portfolio site - $17.16
I run a dog grooming business. I just bought new clippers for $189. Is that just an expense like shampoo, or something else? I want my records to be right.

Something else - and the difference is how long it lasts. Shampoo is consumed: it is used up doing the work, so it sits in supplies. Clippers are a durable tool you will use for years, so they belong on an equipment list with the purchase date, the price, and the receipt kept with it.

The habit that keeps this painless is a written threshold you apply every time, for example: anything over $100 that will last more than a year goes on the equipment list; anything under it, or used up quickly, goes to supplies. The exact threshold is your choice - consistency matters far more than the number, because a rule applied the same way in March and October produces records a stranger can follow.

Whether the $189 is written off all at once or spread over the clippers' life is your accountant's call. Either way, the record they will ask for is the same one: what you bought, when, what it cost, and proof you paid for it.

I clean houses. Yesterday's supply run: bleach $6.49, microfiber cloths $18.99, vacuum bags $14.25, a specialty stone cleaner one client asked for and will pay me back for ($9.80), disposable gloves $11.59, and $42.00 of gasoline for my work van. Organize this for my records.
I'm a personal trainer. I buy protein powder for the shakes I make clients after sessions, and I use some of it myself. It all lands on one receipt. How should I record it?

Split the receipt, and only the business share enters your books. Work out the split on a basis you can defend - tubs bought for the studio shelf versus your kitchen, or servings per week for clients versus yourself - and write that basis on the receipt copy the day you buy it: for example, '3 of 4 tubs for client shakes; 1 personal - $X recorded.'

Then record just the business share as supplies. The personal share is not a business cost with a note attached; it simply never enters the books.

Two habits make this easier next time: buy the studio stock and your own in separate transactions when you can, and keep the split basis the same month to month. An honest, documented estimate beats false precision - what a reviewer wants to see is that a split happened, on a stated basis, at the time, not reconstructed a year later.

Wedding photographer here. This month I bought: SD cards $86.40, a second camera body $1,349.00, my Lightroom plan $11.99, a sample album for the studio shelf $212.50, AA batteries $23.75, and a canvas backdrop $154.30. Sort them the way they should sit in my books.
I have a food truck. My monthly truck payment is $612. Is that an expense in the same way my ingredient purchases are?

No - they are two different kinds of record wearing similar clothes. Ingredients are consumed and gone; each purchase is a straightforward cost of the month. A truck payment is paying down a loan on an asset, and it splits into two parts: interest, which is a cost, and principal, which is not a monthly cost at all - it is you buying the truck, one slice at a time.

So the records look like this: the truck sits on an asset list (what you paid, when you bought it), the loan balance is tracked as it falls, and each $612 payment is recorded as part interest, part loan reduction, using the split on your lender's statement. Recording the whole $612 as a monthly expense overstates your costs and makes the loan invisible.

How the truck's cost is written down over its life is your accountant's territory. Your job is the split and the paperwork - get those right and their job takes ten minutes.

I do plumbing work. Sort today's van-stock purchases: copper fittings $143.20, PVC pipe $67.85, shop towels $12.40, a pipe wrench $38.99, solder $21.30, hand soap $6.75, thread sealant $9.60, and a drain auger $129.00. I want job materials separated from the rest.

I rent a chair in someone else's salon. I pay $700 a month rent and buy all my own color. The salon's backbar shampoo and conditioner are there for everyone and I use them on my clients. A friend says I should record the backbar products as my supplies too, since I use them. Is she right?

She is not. Your records should show what you actually pay for: the $700 rent is your occupancy cost, and the color you buy is your supplies. The backbar products are the salon's cost, bought with the salon's money - the fact that they pass through your hands does not move them into your books.

Recording them anyway would invent expenses you never paid, and it would double-count them across two businesses, since the salon is already recording the same bottles.

The rule of thumb that settles most of these questions: an expense enters your books when money leaves your accounts for it. If you ever start reimbursing the salon for backbar use, that payment - the amount you actually hand over - becomes your expense on that date, recorded as what it is.
I tutor students after school. This month's spending: workbooks $58.20, Zoom subscription $15.99, a whiteboard $34.50, snacks for students $21.35, and parking at the school $8.00. Categorize it.

I'm a landscaper. The mower fuel and the truck fuel both go on the same card at the same gas station, and at tax time it's just a pile of identical 'gas' lines. How do I keep them straight without making my life miserable?

They need separating because they are different records: mower fuel is an operating supply, consumed by the equipment doing the work; truck fuel belongs with vehicle costs, where it sits alongside mileage and tells the vehicle's story.

You do not need a complicated system - you need one rule you will actually follow at the pump. Pick any of these: fill the truck and the mower cans in two separate transactions and write 'truck' or 'mowers' on each receipt; keep a photo of the pump total with a one-word note in your phone; or pay for vehicle fuel with a different card entirely, which makes the split automatic.

What matters is that the split happens the same day, every time. A year of $60 gas lines with no split is not a record - it is a cleanup project waiting for the worst possible weekend.

I run a coffee cart. Last week's purchases: coffee beans $212.00, oat milk $38.45, cups and lids $64.80, propane $27.90, market booth fee $75.00, a new card reader $49.00, and a streaming music subscription for the cart $11.99. Put them where they belong.

I rent a treatment room inside a clinic as a massage therapist. Clients pay the clinic, the clinic keeps 30% for rent and fees, and I get one deposit for the rest. I also sell massage oil blends at the front desk and the clinic adds those sales to my payout. Last month's payout was $2,940. Can I just record $2,940 as my income?

You can, but your books will understate your business in both directions at once - and you will lose information you actually need. The $2,940 is a net figure: it hides your gross session fees and it hides the rent, which is one of your largest costs.

The fuller record, built from the clinic's monthly statement, looks like this: gross session fees recorded as income; the clinic's 30% recorded as rent expense; your oil blends recorded as retail sales, with what the oils cost you as cost of goods. The deposit then reconciles against those three numbers instead of replacing them.

Why it matters beyond tidiness: pricing decisions, a loan application, or selling the practice one day all run on gross revenue and real costs. A book that only shows net deposits can prove money arrived; it cannot show the size of the practice that produced it. Ask the clinic for the itemized monthly statement and file it - the deposit alone, a year from now, proves almost nothing about what it was for.

Web designer. My monthly business charges: client website hosting that I bill back to clients $240.00, Figma $15.00, a stock photo pack $49.00, coworking desk $180.00, a laptop stand $39.99, and my accounting app $30.00. Categorize, with totals.
I'm a copywriter and I write in coffee shops most days. The coffee is basically my office. Can I record my daily coffee as an office expense?

The coffee itself, no - and it is worth understanding why, because the same test settles a dozen similar questions. Coffee is personal sustenance: you would eat and drink something whether or not a client brief was open on the laptop. The work happening next to the cup does not convert the cup into a business cost.

What would be a business cost is paying for the workspace itself - a coworking day pass, or a meeting room the coffee shop rents you for a client session. That charge buys the business something separable from lunch.

The test to carry around: would this purchase exist, in roughly this amount, if no work were happening? If yes, it is personal, even at a desk. Keeping coffee out is not about the money - it is that a year of clean, defensible categories is worth more than a daily $5 line you would have to explain with a straight face.

I'm a mobile mechanic. Today's receipts: brake pads for job #118, $74.20; oil filter for job #119, $11.30; shop rags $16.85; brake cleaner $8.49; nitrile gloves $19.95; my diagnostic tablet subscription $29.99. Sort them.

I teach piano. I buy method books for my students and they pay me back exactly what I paid. I also buy sheet music for my own gigs. At the end of the year my book spending looks huge. How do I record this properly?

You have two different flows tangled in one pile, and they need different homes. The student books are a pass-through: you fronted the money, the student repaid it, the book was never really yours and the money was never really income. Track those in a pass-through line - books bought for students, student repayments - with the student's name on each entry, so the in and the out visibly cancel.

Your own gig music is genuinely yours: that is supplies, or a music library line if the collection keeps growing - pick one home and stay there.

Recorded this way, your year-end picture stops lying: your supply costs show only what your teaching and performing actually consumed, and if a student never repays you, the pass-through line shows exactly who and how much, and the cost becomes yours at that point, with the reason written next to it. The test for any future purchase: if the item and the money both belong to someone else, it goes in the pass-through, not in income or expenses.

Reconcile my business checking for me. The bank statement balance is $4,105.25. Outstanding: check #112 for $212.50 and check #114 for $148.00, neither has cleared. A deposit of $98.00 I made on the 30th is not on the statement. My books say $3,842.75. Return JSON.

```json
{
  "statement_balance": 4105.25,
  "less_outstanding_checks": {
    "#112": 212.5,
    "#114": 148.0,
    "total": 360.5
  },
  "plus_deposits_in_transit": 98.0,
  "adjusted_bank_balance": 3842.75,
  "book_balance": 3842.75,
  "difference": 0.0,
  "reconciled": true
}
```

You reconcile exactly. The two outstanding checks are not errors - they are timing, and they stay on the outstanding list next month until the bank shows them cleared. The deposit in transit is the mirror image: your books have it, the bank does not, yet.

After adjusting for outstanding items, my bank balance works out to $6,389.30, but my books say $6,214.30. Something is off by a round amount. Looking at November: my register shows check #221 to my paper supplier as $475.00, but the bank's cleared-items list shows check #221 at $300.00. Everything else matches. Find the problem and return JSON.

```json
{
  "difference": 175.0,
  "culprit": {
    "entry": "Check #221, paper supplier",
    "recorded_as": 475.0,
    "actual": 300.0,
    "error": "Expense overstated by $175.00 in the books"
  },
  "corrected_book_balance": 6389.3,
  "reconciled_after_correction": true
}
```

Fix the entry itself - change the recorded amount to $300.00 with a note - rather than booking a $175 'adjustment'. A plug would make this month balance while leaving a wrong expense in your records and hiding the next error behind the same trick.

I think I entered some expenses twice - once from the bank feed and once by hand. Here is my October list. Find the duplicate and give me clean totals as JSON.

Oct 2 - Software subscription - $42.99
Oct 5 - Craft supplies - $18.50
Oct 9 - Software subscription - $42.99
Oct 12 - Studio rent share - $120.00
Oct 14 - Design app - $9.99
Oct 18 - Materials - $63.25
Oct 21 - Fuel - $27.40
Oct 24 - Online course - $15.00
Oct 27 - Hand tools - $88.10
Oct 30 - Packaging supplies - $51.19
My bookkeeping app balance never matches my bank balance. Not once, in eight months. What am I doing wrong?

Probably nothing dramatic - the two numbers are not measuring the same thing, so they should not match on a random Tuesday. Your app balance includes everything you have entered: checks written but not yet cleared, deposits recorded but still in transit. The bank only knows about what has posted. On top of that sit card charges that are pending rather than posted, bank fees and interest the app cannot know about until the statement arrives, and the classic duplicate, where the feed imported a charge you had also typed in by hand.

A reconciliation is the monthly ritual that lists exactly those differences, one by one, until every cent is explained by an item with a name and a date. When that list is complete, your books are right - even though the two headline numbers still differ, because now you can say precisely why.

If you have never reconciled, start with the current month rather than excavating all eight. A clean present beats a perfect past.

Full reconciliation, please. Statement balance: $8,942.16. Outstanding checks: $312.44, $89.99, and $1,204.00. Deposits in transit: $750.00. My book balance is $8,120.73. The statement also shows a $45.00 service charge and $10.00 of interest that I have not entered yet. Return the complete two-sided reconciliation as JSON.

```json
{
  "bank_side": {
    "statement_balance": 8942.16,
    "less_outstanding_checks": [
      312.44,
      89.99,
      1204.0
    ],
    "outstanding_checks_total": 1606.43,
    "plus_deposits_in_transit": 750.0,
    "adjusted_bank_balance": 8085.73
  },
  "book_side": {
    "book_balance": 8120.73,
    "less_service_charge_not_yet_entered": 45.0,
    "plus_interest_not_yet_entered": 10.0,
    "adjusted_book_balance": 8085.73
  },
  "difference": 0.0,
  "reconciled": true
}
```

Both sides land on $8,085.73. Note the shape of this one: the bank side needed only timing adjustments, while the book side needed two real entries - the service charge and the interest. Enter those two in the books now, dated as the statement shows them, or next month's reconciliation starts with the same ghosts.

We keep a petty cash tin with a $150 float for the studio. Today I counted $87.40 in cash. The receipts in the tin are: office supplies $18.60, coffee and snacks for a client meeting $23.75, postage $12.25. Reconcile the tin as JSON.
A client swears she paid her invoice two weeks ago. My books show it unpaid and there is no matching deposit in my business account. Where do I look before I embarrass myself by chasing her?

Work through the places money hides, in this order. First, your own app: many systems park received payments in an 'undeposited funds' holding area - recorded as paid, never carried to a bank account, so the invoice and the bank disagree in opposite directions. Second, the wrong account: check whether the deposit landed in your personal account, especially if she pays by transfer and has old details saved. Third, the physical world: a check can sit in a glovebox, a coat, or the envelope it arrived in for a fortnight. Fourth, misapplication: the payment may have been applied to a different invoice of hers, or to a client with a similar name. Fifth, dates: widen the search window - checks get dated when written, deposited when remembered.

If all five come up empty, ask her for what she has - a cleared-check image or a transfer confirmation - framed as 'help me find it at my end', which is both politer and more effective than 'prove it'. Whatever you find, write the outcome on the invoice record. A note that says 'searched undeposited funds, personal account, and paper mail on Nov 26 - not found; client sending confirmation' is a record your future self will thank you for.

My card processor settles in daily batches, gross, and bills fees separately at month end. My POS says this week's card sales were $2,847.60. Deposits that actually arrived: Monday $612.40, Tuesday $588.15, Wednesday $655.90, Thursday $602.35. Friday's batch has not landed yet. Reconcile the week as JSON.

My books record five client payments received in November: A $450, B $275, C $450, D $180, E $320. The bank shows November deposits of $450, $275, $180, and $320. Match them up and tell me what does not fit, as JSON.
I reconciled October and I'm off by $0.37. It's thirty-seven cents. Can I just ignore it?

You can close the month, but do not ignore it silently - and never fix it by nudging some entry by 37 cents to force a match, because that is exactly how a real error gets buried under a cosmetic one.

Give it five minutes first: a difference that small is usually a rounding on a split entry, a fee keyed in a cent off, or a tax-inclusive total divided slightly differently than the bank divided it. Check the two or three largest entries and any split transactions. If it survives the five minutes, book it to a 'rounding and small differences' line with a note - amount, month, and that you looked. That is an honest close.

The exception: if a small difference shows up every month in the same place, it is not rounding, it is a system - a recurring fee you are recording at the wrong amount, or a sales-tax split done two ways. A repeated 37 cents deserves one real investigation; a one-off deserves a note and your evening back.

Hard one. Statement balance: $5,517.42. Outstanding checks: $204.18, $67.50, $431.00. One deposit in transit: $389.26. My book balance is $5,476.00. The statement shows a client's $260.00 check was returned NSF and the bank charged a $12.00 fee - neither is in my books yet. Give me the full reconciliation as JSON.

```json
{
  "bank_side": {
    "statement_balance": 5517.42,
    "less_outstanding_checks": [
      204.18,
      67.5,
      431.0
    ],
    "outstanding_checks_total": 702.68,
    "plus_deposits_in_transit": 389.26,
    "adjusted_bank_balance": 5204.0
  },
  "book_side": {
    "book_balance": 5476.0,
    "less_returned_check_nsf": 260.0,
    "less_bank_fee": 12.0,
    "adjusted_book_balance": 5204.0
  },
  "difference": 0.0,
  "reconciled": true
}
```

Both sides meet at $5,204.00. One follow-through matters more than the arithmetic: the bounced check reopens the client's invoice. The $260 was never truly received, so reverse it against that invoice - putting the balance back into your receivables, where it can be chased - rather than parking it as a miscellaneous expense, where it will be forgotten.

First time reconciling. My statement balance is $1,208.44. I wrote one check, $150.00 to a subcontractor, that has not cleared yet. Nothing else is outstanding. My books say $1,058.44. Did I do it right? Answer as JSON.

```json
{
  "statement_balance": 1208.44,
  "less_outstanding_checks": 150.0,
  "adjusted_bank_balance": 1058.44,
  "book_balance": 1058.44,
  "difference": 0.0,
  "reconciled": true
}
```

You did it right, and you have just performed the whole ritual: take the bank's number, subtract what you have spent that the bank has not seen yet, and arrive at your number. Most months add deposits in transit and the odd fee, but the shape never changes.
I sell on a marketplace platform. My sales report says I sold $3,900 this month, but the deposits into my bank add up to about $3,300. Where did the other $600 go?

Almost certainly nowhere sinister - it was spent on your behalf before the money reached you. The platform's own monthly statement is the bridge document, and it typically reads: gross sales, minus the platform's commission and fees, minus shipping labels bought through the platform, minus refunds to buyers, minus any reserve the platform holds back on new or flagged accounts. What remains is what gets deposited.

The record-keeping point matters more than the missing-money worry: if you record only the deposits as income, your books understate your sales and make your platform fees invisible. Record the gross sales as income, and give each deduction its own line - fees as fees, labels as shipping, refunds as refunds. Then the platform statement reconciles to the bank deposits to the cent, and you can also see what the platform actually costs you, which is a number worth knowing before renewal time.

Reconcile from the platform report monthly, not from the bank feed alone - the bank only ever sees the last step of the journey.

I run a small salon. Reconcile our gift card balance for November as JSON. We started the month with $1,240.00 of gift cards outstanding. During November we sold $860.00 of new cards, clients redeemed $695.00, and one $50.00 card passed the expiry date in our written policy.

```json
{
  "beginning_outstanding": 1240.0,
  "plus_cards_sold": 860.0,
  "less_cards_redeemed": 695.0,
  "less_expired_per_policy": 50.0,
  "ending_outstanding": 1355.0
}
```

The ending figure, $1,355.00, is a liability - money clients have handed you for services you still owe them - not income. Gift card sales become income at redemption, when the service actually happens. Keep the expiry inside this same record, card by card, so the balance can be proven if a client ever disputes it.

I'm a wedding photographer. Clients book with deposits. In October I received: $500 from the Alvarez couple, $750 from the Bennetts, $500 from the Chens, and $1,000 from the Delgados. The Bennett wedding happened on November 14. Show me the state of the deposits as JSON.
My books and my bank reconcile perfectly every month, to the cent. So my records are definitely right, right?

Your cash is definitely right, which is a narrower claim than it sounds. A reconciliation proves exactly one thing: every dollar that moved through the bank account is in your books, once. It says nothing about whether those dollars are in the right categories, whether cash income was recorded at all, whether a personal purchase is sitting in business supplies, or whether you recorded income net of fees so both numbers are smaller than the truth.

A perfectly reconciled set of books can still misdescribe the business completely - the money all arrived and left on schedule, wearing the wrong labels.

The habit that covers the other half is cheap: once a month, read the category totals and ask whether each one looks plausible for your kind of business, and eyeball your ten largest entries. Reconciliation answers 'is all the cash accounted for?' Review answers 'does the story make sense?' You need both questions, and the second one is the one that catches the errors that actually change decisions.
A client just told me my invoice is 'not a proper invoice' and their accounts department won't pay it. All it has is my name, 'website work', and the total. What does a proper invoice actually need?

Your client's accounts department is, annoyingly, right - and each missing element does a specific job. A usable invoice carries: your business name and contact details; the client's name; a unique invoice number; the issue date; a due date stated as an actual date; itemized lines saying what the work was and how it is priced; the total; and how to pay - bank details or a payment link - plus any terms that matter, like a late fee.

The number exists so the invoice can be referenced, tracked, and never paid twice. The due date starts the clock for follow-ups and late fees; 'payable on receipt' starts arguments instead. The itemization is what lets their bookkeeper match your invoice to the work they commissioned - without it, it sits in a pile awaiting someone to vouch for it, which is probably exactly where yours is now.

Fix: send a corrected, complete invoice with a short note, and handle the numbering honestly - either reissue under the same number marked 'corrected', or a new number that references the old one, with a note in your own records either way. Then fix the template, so every future invoice passes the stranger test: could someone who knows nothing about this job pay it without emailing you?

This is the full text of a card receipt from a work purchase. Tell me what it proves and what it does not, as JSON.

FRESH MART
CARD SALE
VISA ****4417
11/08/2026 09:41
TOTAL $86.40
THANK YOU

```json
{
  "proves": {
    "vendor": "Fresh Mart (as printed)",
    "date": "2026-11-08",
    "time": "09:41",
    "amount": 86.4,
    "payment_method": "Visa ending 4417"
  },
  "does_not_prove": [
    "What was bought - there is no item list",
    "That the purchase was for the business",
    "Which job or client it related to",
    "Who made the purchase"
  ],
  "fix": "Write the items and the purpose on it today, while you remember, and photograph it - the card line proves payment happened; your annotation is what makes it a business record."
}
```

This is the general shape of card slips: they are excellent evidence that money moved and nearly silent about why. Every receipt like this needs thirty seconds of handwriting to become a record instead of a rumor.
I've driven to clients all year in my own car and never kept a mileage log. Can I just reconstruct the year from my calendar and call it done?

Mostly yes - if you reconstruct it honestly and keep the evidence you built it from. A usable log needs, per trip: the date, where you went and why (which client or errand), and the miles. Your calendar appointments, invoices with client addresses, and map distances for the routes you actually drove are legitimate sources to rebuild that from.

Two disciplines matter. Mark the log as reconstructed, and keep the sources with it, so anyone reading it can see how each line was derived. And do not invent precision you do not have: use the map distance for the route, rounded sensibly, rather than a suspiciously exact figure for a trip you took in March.

Going forward, the two-minute habit that ends this problem forever: a photo of the odometer, or a one-line note in your phone, at each client stop. And what the finished log is worth at tax time is your accountant's question - the record's job is only to be truthful and checkable, and a sourced reconstruction is both; a confident guess is neither.

For one kitchen remodel job I have these documents: a signed quote for $6,800; my invoice for $6,800; a bank line showing $6,800 received; a text from the client saying 'looks great, thanks!'; dated photos of the finished kitchen; an email from the client approving a $450 tile upgrade mid-job; and a second bank line showing $450 received. Tell me which document proves what, as JSON.
Half my receipts are on thermal paper and they're already fading. By next year they'll be blank. What do I do?

Photograph them the day you get them - a phone scan is fine - and write the purpose on the note or into the filename while it is still fresh: something like 2026-11-26, ToolDepot, $58.25, drill bits for the Alvarez job. Keep the month's photos in one folder (2026-11 receipts) backed up somewhere that is not only the phone.

Once the image exists, the paper can fade in peace; the record cannot.

For the ones already fading: work from the matching card or bank statement line, which still shows the date, vendor, and amount, and annotate what you genuinely remember now - what it was for - marking it as reconstructed. Do that this week rather than at tax time; memory is the perishable part, not just the paper.

This is the invoice I send clients: 'INVOICE - Dana Cole Design. Website services: $900. Please pay promptly. Thank you!' A client's bookkeeper sent it back asking for more detail. What is it missing?

Nearly everything that makes an invoice function as a document rather than a request. It has no invoice number, so neither of you can reference it, and the client cannot be sure they are not paying it twice. It has no date, so the payment clock has no start. 'Pay promptly' is not a due date - the bookkeeper cannot schedule a payment against a sentiment. And '$900 of website services' is not itemized: which site, what work, hours or fixed price? Her system almost certainly needs to match the invoice against something - a quote, a contract, a purchase order - and there is nothing here to match.

Add: your contact details and hers, a unique number, the issue date, a real due date, itemized lines, the total, and how to pay. The test every invoice should pass is that a stranger in an accounts department, who has never heard of you or the job, can pay it correctly without sending it back. Yours failed that test in good company - most first templates do.

My helper submitted an expense claim for a job we did together. Items: taxi fare $23.00 (no receipt - he says the driver did not give one), materials $141.60 (receipt attached), his lunch $17.00 (receipt attached), parking $9.00 (screenshot from the parking app). Tell me what is payable now, what needs more, and what is not payable, as JSON.
My bank and card statements show every payment I make. Isn't that enough of a record on its own?

It is half of a record - the half that proves money moved. A statement cannot say why a payment happened, which job it belonged to, or whether an $86 charge was job supplies, a client gift, or a refund of something. It misses cash entirely. It flattens split purchases - half business, half personal - into one opaque line. And it cannot distinguish a client deposit, which is not yet your income, from earnings, though the two need completely different treatment in your books.

The other half of the record is your annotation: category, purpose, and job, added while you still remember - which is to say, within the week, not the year. Statement plus annotation is a record. Either one alone is a rumor with good handwriting.

The practical version: keep the statements, and spend a few minutes weekly tagging what each line was. That small habit is the entire difference between 'I have statements' and 'I have books'.

Turn this pile of wallet receipts into a clean record. They read: 'Nov 3 - PrintWorks - $24.60 - business cards'; 'Nov 5 - Bean Scene - $13.99 - coffee with client J. Alvarez'; 'Nov 9 - ToolDepot - $58.25 - drill bits'; 'Nov 12 - City Parking - $9.49 - meter at client site'; 'Nov 15 - PaperSource - $112.00 - invoice paper and envelopes'. JSON, with categories and a total.
I built a website for a local bakery. In return, they're catering my launch party. No money is changing hands. My books can just skip the whole thing, right?

They cannot - skipping it makes your records untrue in both directions: you did work that appears nowhere, and you received catering that appears from nowhere. Barter is still an exchange, and the books should show it.

Record both sides at the fair value each of you would charge a stranger: website income on the delivery date, catering as a business expense on the event date, each entry cross-referenced to the other and to a short written agreement stating what was exchanged and the value you both put on it. The values should match each other and should be honest market values, not numbers chosen to make the entry disappear.

Whether and how the exchange is taxed is your accountant's call - but notice that their answer will be built on exactly this record. 'We swapped some stuff' gives them nothing; a dated, valued, written exchange gives them everything. No cash moved. The value still did.

Audit one month of my expense records against my bank statement. My books show eight entries: $120.00, $54.99, $38.40, $210.75, $67.20, $95.00, $29.99, and $45.00 marked 'cash - parking attendant'. The bank statement shows the seven card amounts ($120.00, $54.99, $38.40, $210.75, $67.20, $95.00, $29.99) plus a $6.95 service fee I never entered. Report matches and mismatches as JSON.
Why do people keep telling me to file the signed agreement together with the invoice? The invoice has the amount on it. Isn't that enough?

The invoice states a number; the agreement is what makes the number mean something. Six months from now, the questions that actually arise are never 'what was the total?' - they are 'was that the agreed price, or did it change halfway?', 'was the deposit supposed to be 30% or 50%?', 'the client says the extra visit was included - was it?', and 'they are 40 days late - what did we agree about late payment?' Your invoice answers none of those. The agreement, and any change orders after it, answer all of them.

So file the chain together, per job: agreement, change orders, invoice, proof of payment. The standard to aim for is that a stranger - your future self, your accountant, someone valuing the business - can follow one job's money from promise to payment without having to interview you. An amount floating alone in a folder cannot do that; a chain can.
People keep saying I'm on 'cash basis' and my accountant also mentioned 'accrual'. I did a job on December 20, invoiced it December 21, and got paid January 10. Which year is that income in?

It depends which ruler you measure with, and both rulers are legitimate. Under cash basis, the income belongs to January: money counts when it lands in your account, and it landed on January 10. Under accrual, it belongs to December: income counts when you earned it, and you earned it on December 20 when the work was done and invoiced.

Same job, same dollars, two different birthdays. Neither is an error - they are two conventions about timing, and your accountant picks the one your business files under (most one-person businesses file cash, because it matches the bank account and is simpler to keep).

The thing worth remembering at year-end: a cash-basis December always looks poorer than the work you actually did, because December's work mostly pays in January. That is not your business shrinking; that is the ruler.

Here are five November events. For each one, tell me when it hits the books under cash basis and under accrual basis, as JSON.

1. Nov 3 - I issued an invoice to a client for $750.
2. Nov 9 - A supplier bill for $210 arrived.
3. Nov 18 - The client paid the $750.
4. Nov 25 - I paid the supplier bill.
5. Nov 27 - A new client paid a $400 deposit for work scheduled in December.
My December report says I barely made anything, but January says it was my best month ever. I didn't feel poor in December or rich in January. What is going on?

Nothing is broken - you are watching cash-basis timing do its impression of a business cycle. Your December report counts money that arrived in December, but most of December's work was invoiced late in the month and paid in January. Then January's report collected January's own payments plus December's late arrivals, so it flatters January with two months of effort.

The fix is not necessarily changing how you file - it is changing what you read. Keep a second, simple view alongside the official one: a list of invoices grouped by the month the work was done, and bills by the month they arrived. That earned view is the one to compare month against month, price work by, and judge growth with. Keep the cash view for the question it is actually good at: can I pay the rent on Friday?

Two lenses, two jobs. Most 'my business is mysteriously seasonal' mysteries are one lens being asked to do both.

Compute my November income both ways. Invoices issued in November: $1,200 (paid in November), $800 (paid in December), $450 (still unpaid). Also, in November I received $600 paying off October invoices. JSON, please.

```json
{
  "cash_basis_november_income": 1800.0,
  "cash_basis_breakdown": "1,200 paid in November + 600 received for October work",
  "accrual_basis_november_income": 2450.0,
  "accrual_basis_breakdown": "All work invoiced in November: 1,200 + 800 + 450",
  "difference": 650.0
}
```

Read the difference carefully, because it cuts both ways: the cash view inflates November with $600 of October's work, and hides $1,250 of November work ($800 + $450) that had not been paid yet. Neither number is the lie - but if you judged November's marketing by the cash figure alone, you would be grading October's homework.

I bought $260 of supplies on my business credit card in November and paid the card bill in December. I'm cash basis. Is the expense November or December? And do I record it twice - once for the purchase and once for the payment?

Once, and in November. In ordinary cash-basis bookkeeping the expense lands on the charge date: at the register, the card company paid the store on your behalf, and your purchase was complete at that moment. The December payment to the card company is a transfer - your bank account paying down your card balance - not a second expense. Recording both is the classic way small books quietly double-count a whole season of supplies.

Keep two documents together: the itemized store receipt, which says what you bought, and the card statement, which proves the payment chain. If your accountant prefers the payment-date convention for card purchases, follow them - the unforgivable sin is not November versus December, it is inconsistency, or counting it in both.

December facts: on Dec 28 a client paid me a $900 deposit for a job happening in January. On Dec 30 a supplier bill for $260 arrived, for materials I used in December; I paid it Jan 12. I invoiced $1,400 for December work and was paid on Jan 5. Show me December under the cash view and the accrual view, as JSON.
Should I switch from cash basis to accrual? The business is getting bigger and I feel like I'm flying blind half the time.

Separate two questions that usually arrive glued together: what you file under, and what you steer by. The filing choice has tax consequences, and some businesses are required to use one method or the other - that decision belongs with your accountant, made once, with your real numbers in front of them both.

The steering problem you can fix this week without switching anything. You fly blind because cash reports lag reality: if clients routinely pay 30 to 60 days late, every monthly report is describing the business as it was a month or two ago. Keep an accrual-style dashboard alongside the cash books - invoices grouped by the month the work was done, bills by the month they arrived - and make pricing, hiring, and 'can I afford this' decisions from that view.

Signs accrual thinking is becoming unavoidable rather than optional: you hold real inventory, your receivables are large and slow, or you regularly buy materials months before the job that uses them. If two of those are true, bring the dashboard to your accountant and have the filing conversation with evidence in hand.

Give me the quarter (January to March) both ways. Facts: On Mar 3 I received $950 paying a February invoice. On Mar 10 I invoiced $2,000 and it was paid Mar 20. On Mar 25 I invoiced $1,500 and it was paid Apr 8. Rent of $900 was paid Mar 1. A supplier bill for $400 arrived Mar 15 and was paid Apr 2. On Mar 18 I bought and paid for $275 of supplies. JSON with both nets and an explanation of the difference.

```json
{
  "cash_basis": {
    "income": 2950.0,
    "expenses": 1175.0,
    "net": 1775.0,
    "income_detail": "2,000 paid in March + 950 received for February work",
    "expense_detail": "900 rent + 275 supplies, both paid in March"
  },
  "accrual_basis": {
    "income": 3500.0,
    "expenses": 1575.0,
    "net": 1925.0,
    "income_detail": "Work invoiced in March: 2,000 + 1,500",
    "expense_detail": "900 rent + 400 March bill + 275 supplies"
  },
  "net_difference": 150.0,
  "difference_explained": "Accrual counts the $1,500 March invoice cash misses (+1,500), excludes the $950 of February work cash counts (-950), and counts the $400 March bill cash has not paid yet (-400): 1,500 - 950 - 400 = 150"
}
```

A $150 disagreement on a quarter this size is small - but notice it is built from three four-figure disagreements that nearly cancel. In a quarter where they do not cancel, the two methods will tell you opposite stories about whether you grew.
A client pays me a $1,000 retainer on the first of each month and I work against it. Some months I do $700 of work, some months $1,300. How do I record this without it turning into a mess?

Give the retainer its own bucket with the client's name on it, and stop thinking of the monthly payment as income the moment it arrives. Money in: the bucket goes up by $1,000. Work done: log the date, what it was, and the amount, and draw it down from the bucket. At month-end, whatever is left in the bucket is work you owe (or a refund you owe) - it is the client's money until you earn it.

The $1,300 month is where most retainer arrangements quietly break: the work beyond the bucket is a plain receivable, invoiced as such, not a negative bucket balance everyone forgets. One page per client - date, work, amount, running balance - is the entire system, and it takes two minutes per task.

Without the draw-down log, retainers dissolve into 'I think we're about even', which is where disputes come from - usually in the month the client leaves, when neither of you can prove anything.
I run a small yoga studio. On November 2 a student bought a 10-class pack for $150. By November 30 she had come to 4 classes. Show me how that sits in my records, as JSON.

```json
{
  "pack_price": 150.0,
  "classes_in_pack": 10,
  "value_per_class": 15.0,
  "classes_used_by_nov_30": 4,
  "earned_by_nov_30": 60.0,
  "still_owed_to_student": 90.0,
  "cash_received_in_november": 150.0
}
```

All $150 of cash arrived in November, but the earnings arrive one class at a time - $60 by month-end. The remaining $90 sits in your books as classes owed: a liability, not a problem, but a promise. Studios that spend pack money as if it were all earned in the sale month are borrowing from their own future schedule.
I bought $400 of materials in December for a job that happens in January. Now December looks like a loss and January will look like pure profit. Is my bookkeeping broken?

Not broken - that is cash-basis timing doing exactly what it does, and it will keep doing it every time you buy ahead. The monthly totals are answering the question 'when did money move?', and the honest answer is that $400 moved in December for January's benefit.

The fix for your own understanding is a second tag, not a different method: mark the $400 as belonging to the January job - a job column, a note, whatever your system supports - so the job's own page shows materials $400 plus January labor against the January price. That job page is where you learn whether the work was priced right, and it stays true no matter which month the reports assign things to.

Rule of thumb: let the accounting method decide when things hit the monthly totals, and let job tags decide whether you know what anything earned. You need both answers, and they come from different places.

Two months, both views, income only. December: I invoiced $2,200 - of that, $1,300 was paid in December and $900 was paid in January. I also received $500 in December paying for November work. January: I invoiced $1,600, of which $1,100 was paid in January and the rest was still unpaid at month-end. JSON.

Clients pay me late all the time and I never know what to say or when to say it. Is there a standard way to chase an invoice?

There is a ladder, and climbing it on schedule is most of the secret. A few days before the due date: a friendly flag - 'this is due Friday, here is the payment link again' - which catches the honestly-forgetful while you are still the good guy. On the due date: a short note that it is due today. At 7 days overdue: assume it slipped through - resend the invoice itself, make paying take one click. At 14 days: firmer - name the amount, the original due date, and ask directly whether there is a problem. At 30 days: consequences, whatever your agreement provides - pausing further work is the lever most small businesses actually have.

Every message carries the same four things: invoice number, amount, original due date, and how to pay. And log each send on the invoice record with its date. If a debt ever goes further, that log is your evidence that you were clear, reasonable, and patient - and it stops the 'nobody ever told me' defense cold.

One of my clients is on net-15 terms. Here are their last six invoices with the dates I issued them and the dates they actually paid. Analyze the pattern as JSON.

Issued Jan 5, paid Jan 18 - Issued Feb 3, paid Feb 21 - Issued Mar 4, paid Mar 29 - Issued Apr 2, paid May 3 - Issued May 6, paid Jun 12 - Issued Jun 3, paid Jul 19

```json
{
  "terms_days": 15,
  "days_to_pay": [
    13,
    18,
    25,
    31,
    37,
    46
  ],
  "average_days_to_pay": 28.3,
  "stretch_since_first_invoice": 33,
  "pattern": "Every single invoice was paid later than the one before it - no exceptions, no recovery"
}
```

One late payment is an event; this is a trajectory. A client drifting from 13 to 46 days is slowly borrowing more from you each cycle, and the time to react is while the pattern is visible in the records, not when a payment stops entirely. The usual record-based responses: a deposit before the next job, shorter terms agreed in writing, and work paused at a stated number of days overdue.
A client owed me $1,150 and just paid $600 with a note saying 'rest next month'. How do I record that so the rest does not get lost?

Apply the $600 to the invoice itself - most systems let you record a partial payment against it. The invoice stays open with a $550 balance, and crucially it keeps its original due date: the aging clock does not restart because part of the debt was paid. Note the payment date and the client's 'rest next month' promise on the invoice record, so the follow-up conversation has a paper trail to stand on.

Two things not to do. Do not mark the original invoice paid and issue a fresh $550 invoice - that double-counts the income, resets the debt's age to zero, and makes a 60-day-old obligation look brand new. And do not leave the $600 floating as an unapplied credit, where it will quietly attach itself to the wrong invoice later.

When the rest arrives, it closes the same invoice, and the record will show the whole story: billed once, paid in two parts, on these dates. That story is exactly what you would want if the second part never comes.

I have three open invoices: A for $300 (due Oct 10), B for $450 (due Oct 24), C for $275 (due Nov 7). Today, November 20, the client paid $500 against them generally. Apply it oldest-first and show me what remains, as JSON.
One client is now 60 days late on a $1,900 invoice and wants me to start the next project. I feel awkward about it. What do my records say I should do?

Your records say this is no longer a late payment; it is a pattern with a price tag. Sixty days is two full terms cycles missed, and the request to start new work is asking you to double your exposure to the exact client demonstrating the risk.

The businesslike sequence, all of it easier in writing than in a doorway conversation: first, tie the two facts together in one short message - you are glad to start project two, and the start date is when the $1,900 is settled. Said before work begins, it is a policy; said mid-project, it is a crisis. Second, when they do re-engage, the new agreement carries a deposit and a pause-work clause, so the next conversation is pre-written. Third, look at their trend rather than this single invoice - a client sliding from 15 to 45 to 60 days is telling you something about their cash, and your records are the only place that story is written down.

Awkward once beats unpaid twice. And keep every step on the client record, so if the story continues you are not reconstructing it from memory.

Clean up my receivables list. It currently shows: #201 - $210 open; #202 - $340 open; #203 - $525 open; #204 - $180 open; #205 - $180 open. But my bank shows a $340 deposit on Nov 12 from the #202 client, and looking closer, #205 is the same client, same job, and same date as #204 - I think I invoiced that job twice. Fix the list as JSON.
I take a 50% deposit before starting a job and invoice the rest at the end. But my receivables report looks like clients owe me double what they actually do. What am I doing wrong?

Almost certainly, you are issuing two full documents for one job: a deposit invoice for the 50%, and then a final invoice for the whole price - so the books believe the job was sold twice, once at half price and once at full. Your receivables are faithfully adding up the fiction.

Two clean patterns; pick either. Pattern one: a single invoice for the full price, with the deposit recorded as a payment against it the day it arrives - the balance then reads as the remaining 50% from the start. Pattern two: the deposit is recorded as 'deposit held' when it arrives, and applied to the final invoice when that is issued. Either way, the job has exactly one price in your books, and the deposit is a payment event, not a second sale.

The test for your report afterward: receivables should show only what clients still owe you - money not yet paid for work billed. If a number on there has already been collected once, it is not a receivable; it is a bookkeeping echo.

Full receivables workup for my design studio, as of today, November 26, 2026. Open invoices: Northwind - Inv 301, due Nov 30, $1,800, nothing paid. Northwind - Inv 288, due Oct 15, $950, nothing paid. Bluebird Cafe - Inv 295, due Nov 10, $620, $310 paid. Bluebird Cafe - Inv 276, due Sep 1, $480, nothing paid. Hartley Law - Inv 299, due Nov 20, $2,300, nothing paid. Hartley Law - Inv 282, due Sep 22, $1,150, nothing paid. Moss & Vine - Inv 270, due Aug 5, $760, nothing paid. Moss & Vine - Inv 304, due Dec 10, $540, nothing paid. Bucket the balances, total by client, and name the biggest risk. JSON.
A client from March never paid his $680 invoice and has now gone out of business. A friend who does bookkeeping said to 'just write it off'. What does that actually mean in my books?

In the ledger it means closing the file honestly: mark the invoice uncollectible, with the date and the reason - 'client ceased trading, written off November 2026' - and move it out of your open receivables, so your AR stops pretending that $680 is on its way.

What it does not mean is deleting anything. The invoice, the record of the work, your follow-ups, and the write-off note all stay in the file. If the client resurfaces or a liquidator pays a percentage, you will be very glad the trail exists.

What the write-off does for your taxes is a separate question, and it belongs to your accountant - the bookkeeping act and the tax treatment are cousins, not twins. Your part is the truthful record: billed, chased, uncollectible, closed. Accountants can work with that. What nobody can work with is an invoice that quietly vanished in March and left your totals unexplained.

Today is November 26, 2026. I use a follow-up ladder: a friendly resend at 7 days overdue, a firmer note at 14, a serious notice at 30, and a final notice after that. Assign each invoice its step: Inv A - $425 - due Nov 19. Inv B - $780 - due Nov 12. Inv C - $1,150 - due Oct 27. Inv D - $260 - due Oct 2. JSON.
A client says two lines on my invoice are wrong and is refusing to pay any of it until we sort it out. The invoice is $2,300 and the disputed lines total $350. How should I handle the record?

First, do not edit the invoice. It has been issued; rewriting it destroys the trail and makes both parties' records disagree about what was originally billed. The original stays exactly as sent.

Second, split the invoice in your records and in your correspondence into its two real parts: $1,950 undisputed, which is still due and still aging - say so plainly and politely, because 'I dispute a line' is not a discount on the rest - and $350 disputed, with the date and the substance of the disagreement noted on the invoice record.

Then resolve the $350 on its merits. If the client is right, issue a credit note for $350 against the invoice rather than altering it: the books then show what was billed, what was contested, and what was conceded, as three facts with three dates. If you are right, the original stands and the correspondence is your evidence. Either way, the record tells the whole story to anyone who reads it later - including, if it ever comes to it, someone deciding the matter for you.

Build the draw-down ledger for a consulting retainer. The client paid a $3,000 retainer on October 1. My rate is $120 an hour. Work done: Oct 6 - 4.5 hours; Oct 13 - 3 hours; Oct 21 - 6.25 hours; Oct 28 - 2.5 hours. JSON with a running balance.
My invoices say 'Net 30'. One client told me he thought that meant he pays at the end of the following month, and another pays 30 days after she gets back from vacation. How do I stop this?

Print an actual due date on the invoice - 'Due: December 12, 2026' - and let the term ride along as decoration if you like. 'Net 30' is trade shorthand that civilians genuinely read three different ways, as your two clients just demonstrated; a calendar date has exactly one reading, and it is the date your follow-up ladder, any late fee, and any dispute will run from.

While you are fixing the template, put the other ambiguity-killers on it too: the invoice number, the total in figures, and a payment link or bank details, so 'I wasn't sure how to pay' dies as an excuse as well.

If a client's own accounts department pays on a fixed cycle - say, the 15th for everything received by the 1st - that is worth knowing before the work starts and writing into the agreement. Payment timing discovered at day 45 is a surprise; the same timing agreed at day 0 is just terms.
Everything runs through my personal checking account - client payments, groceries, business subscriptions, my studio rent, all of it mixed together. My records are a nightmare. Where do I even start?

Do not start with the past - start by damming the flow. This week: open a business account, point every client payment to it, and move every business subscription and card onto it. From Friday, one rule with no exceptions: nothing business touches the personal account, and nothing personal touches the business one.

The mixed history stays as it is. That feels wrong, but it is the right order: an accountant can work with a messy past that has stopped growing; nobody can fix a mess that adds new entries daily. Within a month, the new account's statement effectively is your business record, and the weekly habit of categorizing a clean feed takes minutes instead of a weekend.

If money needs to move between you and the business - and it will - do it as visible transfers labeled owner contribution or owner draw. The one-account era ends not with a cleanup project but with a border, defended daily, that costs nothing to keep.

This is one month of my only bank account - business and personal all mixed. Sort it: client payment received $1,150.00; craft fair booth fee $86.40; groceries $132.18; design software $54.99; daycare $210.00; work boots $39.95; coffee with a client $18.20; gasoline $64.00; streaming subscription $29.99; materials order $425.00. JSON with totals.
I have three years of receipts in a shoebox and nothing entered anywhere. Do I have to do all of it before I can start keeping books properly?

No - and believing you do is exactly why the shoebox keeps winning. Draw a line at the first of this month, or this quarter if that feels more honest, and keep perfect books forward from there. The present is the only part you fully control.

Then backfill only what already has a skeleton: your bank and card statements carry dates, vendors, and amounts for the current year even if you recorded nothing. Enter those at statement level, so the year has a true shape, and let the shoebox serve as supporting evidence for entries the statements already prove - the receipt that explains what the $86.40 at the supply store actually was. That turns three years of dread into a few evenings of matching.

Older years stay boxed and labeled by year. If your accountant ever needs them, you will dig with a specific question in hand, which is a completely different task from data-entering a shoebox on spec. Forward-only first, statement-level backfill second, perfection never.

Apply a month-end close to my one-person design business for November and tell me what is not done. Facts: my last November invoice is #147, issued Nov 29. My bank feed is imported through Nov 28. Two receipts from Nov 30 are still unphotographed in my wallet. A supplier bill for $210 arrived Nov 26 and is unpaid. A client payment of $500 arrived Nov 30 and I have not matched it to an invoice yet. Return the close checklist as JSON.
Every month I transfer $2,000 from my business account to myself and record it as a salary expense. My profit looks terrible. A friend says that is not an expense at all. Who is right?

Your friend - assuming you are a sole proprietor, which the setup suggests. In a sole proprietorship you and the business are the same taxpayer, so paying yourself is not a cost of running the business; it is you taking the profit out. The $2,000 transfers are owner draws, and they belong in a draw account, not in expenses.

Recording them as salary does two kinds of damage at once: your profit is understated by $24,000 a year, so every decision you make from those reports - pricing, hiring, whether the business works at all - is based on a business that looks $24,000 worse than reality. And the draw itself becomes invisible, so you cannot see what you actually took.

Recorded properly you get the two numbers you genuinely need, separately: what the business earned, and what you took out of it. If you were an employee of your own company the answer would be different - that is an entity question for your accountant - but in a sole prop's books, the profit already is your pay; the draw is just the moving of it.

I sweep a percentage of everything that lands in my operating account: 25% to a tax-holding savings account and 10% to a materials reserve. This week's deposits were Monday $840, Wednesday $1,260, Friday $975. Do this week's sweep as JSON.

In November I paid six business bills from my personal account because the business account was new and empty: print shop $214.30, software $89.99, studio rent $1,150.00, courier $67.45, materials $320.00, parking permits $48.60. My bookkeeper says these still belong in the business books. Show me the records to enter, as JSON.
I do photograph my receipts, but my camera roll is chaos and I can never find the one I need. Give me a system I will actually keep up.

The system has one rule with three small parts: the photograph gets a name before your phone goes back in your pocket. Date, vendor, amount, purpose - '2026-11-26, ToolDepot, 58.25, drill bits, Alvarez job'. Thirty seconds, at the counter, while the purpose is still obvious to you. That filename is the filing system: searchable by vendor when the card statement puzzles you, by amount when you are reconciling, by job when a client questions a cost.

Once a week - pick the day you already do invoices - move the week's receipt photos into a folder named by month, somewhere that syncs off the phone. That is the whole system. Thermal receipts get photographed the same day without exception, because they are the ones already fading.

The test to apply to any system, including this one: can you find the receipt for a specific charge in under a minute, six months from now, starting from nothing but the charge? If yes, you have records. If no, you have a photo collection with business aspirations.

My expense categories have grown wild. I currently have: Supplies, Materials, Shop stuff, Misc, Office, Office supplies, Gas, Fuel, Car, Ads, Marketing. Consolidate them into a list I can actually maintain, as JSON with the mapping.
I'm selling my small service business. The buyer keeps asking for 'clean books'. What does that actually mean, concretely? What will they look at?

They will try to follow your money without you in the room, and 'clean' means they succeed. Concretely, expect them to test: bank statements that reconcile to the books, month by month, for at least the last two years; a receivables list where every open invoice is real, current, and explained in a sentence; an equipment list with purchase dates and costs for everything the price assumes they are buying; recurring costs visible as themselves - rent, subscriptions, insurance - rather than scattered through supplies; and owner draws separated from business expenses, so the true profit stands naked.

That last one is where sellers quietly lose money: a business is usually priced as a multiple of its profit, so every personal item hiding in expenses lowers the apparent profit and therefore the price - you pay for the muddle twice, once in confusion and once in valuation.

Nothing on their list requires better software. It requires that the story your numbers tell - what came in, what it cost, what is still owed, what you own - can be verified by a stranger from documents alone. If a number in your books needs you standing next to it explaining, it is not clean yet.

Design my weekly bookkeeping routine. I'm a mobile dog groomer. In a typical week I have about 25 card payments from clients (they import automatically), about 6 supply purchases, 3 invoices to kennels I contract with, and cash tips on some days. I want it to take about half an hour, once a week. JSON.
Some of my clients pay cash. Honestly, some of it never makes it into my books - it goes in my pocket and gets spent. How bad is that, and how do I fix the habit?

It is the most common hole in small-business records, and it distorts more than the missing amount: income is understated, any supplies bought with that cash vanish as expenses too, and your bank account loses the ability to tell your business's story - which matters the first time you need it to, for a loan, a dispute, or a valuation.

The fix is mechanical, not moral, and it has two parts. Log the cash the day it arrives: client, invoice, amount - a dated line in your phone notes is a legitimate start. And deposit it intact: do not spend from undeposited cash, because that is precisely where the trail dies - money that never reaches the bank leaves no independent witness.

If you need pocket money, take it afterward as a recorded owner draw from the business account, which is the same cash living an honest life. Deposit intact, log same day. Two habits, and the hole closes without a single lecture from your accountant.

Here is my October expense ledger as recorded: Oct 3 - Supplies - $54.00; Oct 7 - Software - $15.99; Oct 12 - Materials - $132.40; Oct 15 - Fuel - $48.20; Oct 21 - Training - $75.00; Oct 26 - Tools - $89.95; Oct 30 - Booth fee - $60.00; Oct 31 - Equipment rental - $210.00. Recorded total: $685.54. But I have checked the sources: the Oct 3 receipt actually says $45.00, and the equipment rental was picked up and invoiced on Nov 2, not in October. Give me the corrected picture as JSON.

```json
{
  "errors_found": [
    {
      "entry": "Oct 3 - Supplies",
      "recorded": 54.0,
      "actual": 45.0,
      "type": "Transposed digits",
      "overstatement": 9.0
    },
    {
      "entry": "Oct 31 - Equipment rental",
      "recorded": 210.0,
      "actual_month": "November (invoiced Nov 2)",
      "type": "Wrong month",
      "overstatement_to_october": 210.0
    }
  ],
  "recorded_october_total": 685.54,
  "corrected_october_total": 466.54,
  "total_overstatement": 219.0
}
```

Fix both errors at their source - change the entry, move the entry - rather than adding a compensating 'correction' line that leaves the two mistakes in place and makes the ledger tell three stories. And note the shapes: a transposition (54 for 45) and a month-boundary slip are the two most common ledger errors there are; knowing their faces is most of proofreading.
I make my invoices in a word processor and number them roughly as I go. I just noticed there is no invoice #108 anywhere - 107 and 109 exist. Does a gap like that actually matter?

It matters because sequential numbering is the cheapest internal control you own, and a gap is that control reporting for duty. A missing number means one of three things: the invoice was voided - fine, if the voided copy is still in the file marked VOID; it was issued outside your system - a document that never got logged, which can mean income your books never saw; or it is a numbering slip and nothing is missing at all. All three are worth knowing, and they are distinguished by ten minutes of checking: look at which clients hold 107 and 109, and whether any work from that week lacks an invoice.

Going forward the rules are short: numbers issued in order, never reused, voids kept and marked rather than deleted. When every number is accounted for, you can prove your invoice list is complete - and completeness is the thing you will want proven the first time a client insists they were never billed, or you cannot tell whether you were ever paid.
Can I deduct my truck? I use it for my landscaping business about 80% of the time.

That question - what you may deduct - is one I will not answer here, because it turns on rules, your entity type, and your specific facts, and a confident wrong answer is expensive. What I can do is make the question answerable in a single sitting with your accountant, which is the part people actually get stuck on.

Bring three things. A mileage log for a representative period showing business versus personal use - your 80% should be the log's conclusion, not an estimate offered from memory. The purchase or lease documents plus the running costs - fuel, repairs, insurance - gathered in one vehicle file. And the truck's other uses stated plainly, including the personal share.

With those records, the accountant's answer takes minutes and rests on something that holds up. Without them, even a 'yes' is built on sand, because the deduction is only ever as good as the log underneath it. My job is the log. Their job is the answer.
My friend writes off everything - his home office, his truck, he even jokes his dog guards the shop. He says I'd be stupid not to do the same. I keep my records pretty plain. Am I doing it wrong?

You are doing the part that is yours exactly right. What gets claimed on a return is a decision between a taxpayer and their accountant, informed by their facts and their appetite for risk - it is genuinely not a bookkeeping question, and your friend's confidence is not evidence about your situation.

What you control is whether your records say what actually happened: real dates, real amounts, a purpose a stranger can follow. A record like that serves you in every version of the future. If you and your accountant decide to claim something, the record supports it. If you do not, the record still proves your numbers for running the business, which is its first job.

The day records get 'creative' is the day they stop being useful for that first job - you can no longer trust your own reports, because you know which lines are theater. Keep yours plain and complete. Your friend can keep his dog.
A client paid me in November but asked me to date the invoice in October so it lands in his budget year. It's the same money either way - can you just make the invoice say October 28?

No - and the reason is not pedantry. An invoice dated October 28 for billing that happened in November states something untrue, and both sets of books then inherit it: his October expenses and your October income would both record an event in a month when it did not occur. If the dates are ever examined, 'the client asked me to' is not a defense that improves with age.

What can be done, all of it legitimate: issue the invoice today, dated today, with a service-period line - 'work performed October 12-24' - which is true, and which most budget systems actually key on, since what they usually need is the work in the right period, not the paper. If his finance department insists the document itself must carry an October date, that is a decision for them to request in writing and own on their side.

Your records should be boring and accurate. They are the one thing that protects you when two people's memories of an arrangement start to differ.
I just started selling my ceramics at markets. Am I supposed to charge sales tax on them? And if I collect it, is that money income?

Whether you must collect it is a tax-rules question - it depends on your state, what exactly you sell, and where you sell it - and it is worth getting right before your first market rather than after your tenth. That answer belongs to your accountant or your state's small-business guidance, not to me.

The second half is pure record-keeping, and I can answer it completely: tax you collect is never income. It is money you are holding for the state, passing through your hands. From the very first dollar, it should live in its own line - 'sales tax collected, held' - separate from your sales figures, so your reports never flatter you with money that was never yours.

The businesses that get hurt here are the ones where collected tax quietly spends like revenue all quarter, and then the remittance date arrives. A separate line from day one makes that accident structurally impossible.
For my car, should I track mileage or just keep all the vehicle receipts? Which one is better for me?

Better is a computation, and it should be run on your numbers by your accountant - the winner depends on how much you drive for work, what the car costs to run, and your situation, none of which a general answer can see. What I can tell you is how to make the question answerable instead of eternal.

For one quarter, keep both records: a simple mileage log - date, client or errand, miles - and every vehicle receipt, fuel, repairs, insurance, kept together in a vehicle folder. Neither is onerous for three months. At quarter-end, your accountant can run both methods against the same real quarter and tell you which produces the better result and which record to keep maintaining.

Most people guess with no data and then track the losing method beautifully for years. One quarter of double-tracking buys you a permanent, evidence-based answer - and whichever way it lands, you will already have the habit the answer requires.
I'm hiring my first helper for my cleaning business, two days a week to start. Should she be a contractor or an employee? I need to know what paperwork to do.

The classification itself is a legal and tax determination - it turns on how much control you exercise over how she works, not on which label is cheaper or simpler - and getting it wrong is genuinely costly in back payments and penalties. That call belongs to your accountant or an employment professional, and it should be made before her first shift, not reconstructed after her fiftieth.

What starts now, whichever way the determination lands, is the record-keeping - and it is the same list either way. A written agreement that states what was decided and the basis for it. A log of her hours and which jobs she worked. Every payment recorded with date, amount, and method - no cash-in-an-envelope invisibility, which protects you as much as her. And her tax details collected on the proper form at the start, not chased in a panic in January.

Records do not decide the classification. But they are what prove you ran whichever arrangement you chose, properly - and in any later dispute about it, the side with the contemporaneous paper usually wins.
I'm a sole proprietor. Can I put myself on payroll, pay myself a salary, and deduct it as a business expense? It would make my books look cleaner.

It would make them look cleaner and be wrong, which is a bad trade. In a sole proprietorship, you and the business are the same taxpayer - there is no separate 'you' for the business to employ. Money you move to yourself is an owner draw, and the business's profit is already your income whether you move it or not. Recording a salary to yourself would invent an expense and understate the profit by the same amount, so your reports would flatter your tax position and mislead your decisions at the same time.

If the payroll idea appeals for real reasons - a steady paycheck rhythm, retirement contributions, bringing on other people - that is an entity conversation, about elections and structures that genuinely change the answer. It is squarely your accountant's territory, and it is a good conversation to have with your draw history in hand.

Meanwhile, the honest version is also the simple one: transfers to yourself, labeled as draws, every time. Clean books are books that tell the truth plainly, not books with extra lines in them.
How much should I be setting aside for taxes? So far this year I've taken in $18,400 and spent $6,150 on the business.

The percentage itself is advice I will not invent for you - it depends on your total income picture, your entity, your state, and your deductions, and the honest version of the answer is a five-minute calculation by an accountant looking at your actual situation. Anyone who names you a percentage from those two numbers alone is guessing with your money.

What I can give you is the number to carry into that conversation: your profit so far is $18,400 minus $6,150, which is $12,250 - and profit, not takings, is the figure any set-aside percentage applies to. People who set aside a percentage of everything that lands routinely over-save in fat months and under-save in lean ones; the profit figure is the real base.

The records habits that make this painless once you have your percentage: a separate savings account the set-aside sweeps into every time money lands, so it is never sitting in operating looking spendable, and the quarterly due dates on your calendar now, so a deadline is never a surprise. Percentage from the accountant, machinery from the books.

I'm a freelance translator. Some clients pay me in euros, some in dollars. My bank converts the euros when they arrive. How do I record the euro invoices so my books stay sane?

Record each invoice in the currency it was issued in - client, date, and the euro amount as invoiced. When the payment lands, record the dollars actually received next to it, and keep the bank's conversion advice with the invoice: it shows the rate applied and any fee, and it is the bridge document between the two numbers.

Two rules keep the books sane. Never record a euro amount as if it were dollars - it is the classic silent error in mixed-currency books, and it inflates income by the exchange rate. And let the difference between the invoice's value and the dollars received appear as its own small, labeled line rather than fudging the invoice figure to match the deposit; the invoice says what you charged, the bank line says what arrived, and the gap has a name.

What that gap means for your taxes is your accountant's question. The record's job is just to show all three numbers honestly, and with the conversion advice filed, it does.

I keep my books up to date but I never actually look at them. What should a monthly review involve for a business my size?

Five numbers, fifteen minutes, the same day each month. First, money in - what actually arrived; it tells you whether the business is growing or coasting. Second, money out by category, but only the top two categories - surprises live there, and the long tail can look after itself. Third, your receivables total and, separately, the single oldest unpaid invoice: the total is the business's health, the oldest one is the fire. Fourth, balances - what the accounts hold, with anything held for others (client deposits, gift cards outstanding, tax collected) mentally fenced off, because that portion is not yours to spend however healthy the balance looks. Fifth, one comparison: this month against the same month last year, or against your running average. A single month means almost nothing; a direction means a great deal.

Write the five numbers down where last month's sit next to them - a notebook page beats a dashboard you will stop opening. That is the entire review. Everything fancier is decoration until these five are a habit, and once they are, you will find you are running the business from your records instead of merely storing them.
